summary: An April 1st joke RFC claiming that quantum entanglement will give some internet paths a round-trip time of zero seconds, a case protocol designers never expected, and warning of a bug worse than the millennium bug. It is humor, not a real problem report.

eli5.summary: A joke about messages arriving at the very same instant they are sent, which would confuse every computer. Made for April Fools' Day.

questions: what is the quantum bug rfc
is there an april fools rfc about quantum networking
what protocols fail with zero rtt
subtitle: What happens when quantum entanglement gives internet packets zero round-trip time.

tldr.problem: Quantum networks using entanglement can transfer information instantly with zero delay between peers. This is a scenario no internet protocol was designed to handle.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs protocols that will fail when round-trip time becomes zero: LEDBAT will send endlessly, MPTCP will divide by zero, and RTP will crash. It warns this is a bigger problem than the year 2000 bug.
tldr.outcome: This April Fools RFC jokes that quantum networks are arriving soon and will break the internet unless specifications are updated. No actual quantum internet exists yet.

today: RFC 8774 is an April Fools RFC published in 2020 for informational purposes. Quantum networks at internet scale do not exist and the scenario remains speculative.

sections.title: The Impossible Scenario
sections.content:
This April Fools RFC imagines that quantum networking using entanglement will soon become the standard internet technology. Quantum entanglement can transfer a state (bit) instantly with no delay, meaning a path between two quantum computers would have a round-trip time (RTT) of zero seconds.

The RFC notes that this scenario is not actually predicted in most protocol specifications. TCP has TCP Fast Open and TLS 1.3 support zero-RTT, but many older protocols were never designed to handle messages arriving faster than they could possibly respond to them.
sections.eli5: Messages travel instantly with no delay. That sounds good, but protocols expect messages to take at least a tiny bit of time to arrive, so they will break.

sections.title: Protocols That Will Crash
sections.content:
The RFC describes three concrete failures: LEDBAT (Low Extra Delay Background Transport) measures delay to throttle itself, but with zero RTT, delay samples become zero. Its target is 100 milliseconds, which it will never reach; it will endlessly increase its send window until the limit of representable bits is exhausted, then send data as fast as it can.

Multipath TCP calculates a value called alpha by dividing by RTT squared and RTT, leading to division by zero. RTP Circuit Breakers have a simplified equation that divides by RTT; with RTT = 0, this produces division by zero and crashes multimedia applications.

The RFC notes that TCP itself survives because its retransmission timeout is lower-bounded at 1 second, and flow control limits its send rate.
sections.eli5: Protocols that measure how long messages take to arrive cannot work when messages arrive instantly. Some will try to divide by zero and crash; others will send data as fast as they can and overwhelm the network.

sections.title: The Urgent Warning
sections.content:
The RFC warns that protocols need to add two defenses: never divide by RTT, and use flow control on all paths. UDP and ICMP will need receiver windows. All RFCs containing "0-RTT mistakes" need to be found and updated urgently.

The security section notes that on a zero-RTT path, an attacker could send a denial-of-service flood that arrives all at once, completely overwhelming a sender. Flow control, which limits how much data a receiver can accept, is the only defense.
sections.eli5: Before this breaks the internet, all protocols must be fixed to not divide by zero and to limit how much data arrives at once.

sections.title: The Point of the Joke
sections.content:
RFC 8774 is written in earnest technical language, describing a cascade of catastrophic failures as if they were imminent. The humor comes from treating an absurd scenario (quantum networks deployed worldwide in five to ten years) as inevitable, and calmly discussing how to fix the "Quantum Bug" as something urgent.

Published April 1, 2020, as informational, the RFC is purely humorous. Quantum networks may eventually become real, but the scenario of instant internet-scale communication is purely speculative.
sections.eli5: It jokes about a future problem that probably will never happen, but describes it as seriously as if it were about to break everything tomorrow.
